Chapter 8: Weaving the Principles Together—the SUCCESs Checklist in Practice
Now that we've explored all six principles—Simplicity, Unexpectedness, Concreteness, Credibility, Emotions, and Stories—let's talk about what really happens when you put them into action.
Imagine the SUCCESs framework as your very own communication toolkit. Sometimes, you'll reach for one tool over another, depending on your message or audience. But here’s the thing—the most powerful ideas usually blend several of these principles all at once.
Take a public service announcement, for example. What if it used a message that's simple and concrete, told through a surprising story? Add in a dash of strong emotion and back it up with credible facts—and suddenly, you’ve got a message that really sticks.
When you’re applying the SUCCESs framework, it helps to run through a mental checklist. Think of it like a quick self-check as you craft your message:
Is your core message clear and simple? Does it grab attention in a way that's truly unexpected? Are your details concrete—can people actually picture what you're saying? Is your message credible and trustworthy? Does it make people feel something? And finally, is your idea wrapped up in a story that people will remember?
Let’s look at a real-world example. Think about those campaigns encouraging folks to wear seatbelts. The slogan “Click it or ticket” is simple and concrete—hard to forget. Those unexpected visuals, like a slow-motion video of a crash, really make you pay attention. Add credibility with statistics and endorsements from safety experts. Then, bring in emotion by showing the impact on families affected by accidents. And of course, stories from real survivors can move people to action.
The real secret? Blending these principles naturally, without forcing it. Sure, not every message will check all six boxes. But the more you can weave in, the stickier your idea becomes.
Over time, as you practice thinking this way, it’ll start to feel effortless. You’ll find yourself crafting messages that stick—messages people remember and act on.
